        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis.

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script). It covers everything you asked for: | Step | What to do | Command / File | |------|------------|----------------| | 1 | **Clone the repo** | `git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` | | 2 | **Analyse & create files** | – Dockerfile
– Kubernetes YAMLs
– GitHub Actions workflow | | 3 | **Stage the new files** | `git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml` | | 4 | **Commit & push** | `git commit -m "Add Docker, K8s, CI files"`
`git push origin main` | --- ## 2.1 Dockerfile Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content: ```dockerfile # Use the official Node.js 18 slim image as the base FROM node:18-slim # Set metadata LABEL maintainer="Your Name " LABEL description="Docker image for the nodejs-welcome app" # Create app directory WORKDIR /usr/src/app # Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache COPY package*.json ./ # Install dependencies RUN npm ci --only=production # Copy the rest of the source code COPY . . # Expose the port the app listens on EXPOSE 3000 # Default command CMD ["node", "app.js"] ``` > **Why this Dockerfile?** > * `node:18-slim` is small, stable, and contains the latest LTS Node.js. > * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from `package-lock.json`. > * The app is assumed to listen on port **3000** (the common default for Express apps). > * If your app uses a different entry point or port, adjust the `EXPOSE` and `CMD` lines accordingly. --- ## 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs Create a directory called `k8s` (or any name you prefer) and add two files: ### `k8s/deployment.yaml` ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: nodejs-welcome-deployment labels: app: nodejs-welcome spec: replicas: 2 selector: matchLabels: app: nodejs-welcome template: metadata: labels: app: nodejs-welcome spec: containers: - name: nodejs-welcome image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest # <-- change if you use another registry ports: - containerPort: 3000 env: - name: NODE_ENV value: production resources: limits: cpu: "500m" memory: "256Mi" requests: cpu: "250m" memory: "128Mi" ``` ### `k8s/service.yaml` ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: nodejs-welcome-service spec: type: ClusterIP selector: app: nodejs-welcome ports: - protocol: TCP port: 80 # Service port targetPort: 3000 # Container port ``` > **What this does** > * The Deployment runs **2 replicas** of your app. > * The Service exposes the pods on port **80** inside the cluster (you can change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access). > * The image reference (`ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`) assumes you’ll push the image to GitHub Container Registry. Replace it with Docker Hub or another registry if you prefer. --- ## 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow Create the directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file named `ci.yml`: ```yaml name: Build & Push Docker Image on: push: branches: - main jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Checkout repository uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Set up Docker Buildx uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3 - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry uses: docker/login-action@v3 with: registry: ghcr.io username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} - name: Build and push Docker image uses: docker/build-push-action@v5 with: context: . push: true tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest # Optional: add a tag with the commit SHA # tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest,ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }} - name: Image digest run: echo "Image pushed with digest ${{ steps.docker_build.outputs.digest }}" ``` ### What the workflow does 1. **Trigger** on pushes to `main`. 2. Checks out the repo. 3. Sets up Docker Buildx (multi‑platform support). 4. Logs into GitHub Container Registry using the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN`. 5. Builds the Docker image from the root `Dockerfile` and pushes it to `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`. 6. Prints the image digest for debugging. > **Prerequisites** > * The repo must be hosted on GitHub (which it is). > * No extra secrets are needed because `GITHUB_TOKEN` is automatically provided. > * If you want to push to Docker Hub instead, replace the login and tags accordingly. --- ## 3. Stage the new files ```bash git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml ``` ## 4. Commit & push ```bash git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow" git push origin main ``` --- ### Quick sanity check After pushing, you should see: * A new **Actions** tab with a successful run. * In the **Packages** section of your GitHub repo, the Docker image `nodejs-welcome:latest` should appear. * You can deploy the app to a cluster with: ```bash kubectl apply -f k8s/ ``` --- **That’s it!** You now have a fully‑functional Docker image, Kubernetes deployment/service, and CI pipeline that automatically builds and publishes the image whenever you push to `main`. Happy coding!
